about: Curated list for the Assist app's Safety mode. 'words' are what the text reader looks for on a label (lower case; longest phrase wins). 'formulas' are matched against printed or handwritten chemical formulas. 'tags' are what the rules below pair up. 'removes' cancels tags on the same package ("alcohol free"). Edit freely; tests/test_safety_kb.py checks the file is consistent. This is general safety information, not medical or professional advice.

substances.name: Bleach
substances.note: Burns skin and eyes. Use with a window open and never mix it with other cleaners.

substances.name: Pool chlorine / bleaching powder
substances.note: Strong oxidiser: can start a fire in contact with oils, fuels or organic matter. Keep dry.

substances.name: Ammonia cleaner
substances.note: Irritating fumes. Ventilate well.

substances.name: Glass cleaner (often contains ammonia)
substances.note: Many glass cleaners contain ammonia. Check the label before using it near bleach.

substances.name: Acid toilet cleaner
substances.note: Most are strong acids (often hydrochloric acid). Never use together with bleach.

substances.name: Hydrochloric acid
substances.note: Corrosive liquid and fumes. Work in a fume cupboard or with good ventilation.

substances.name: Sulfuric acid
substances.note: Causes severe burns. Always add acid to water, never water to acid.

substances.name: Nitric acid
substances.note: Corrosive and a strong oxidiser. Keep away from anything organic or flammable.

substances.name: Vinegar (acetic acid)
substances.note: A weak acid. Safe as food; concentrated acetic acid is corrosive.

substances.name: Drain cleaner (caustic soda)
substances.note: Causes severe burns and gets hot with water. Never follow one drain cleaner with a different one.

substances.name: Potassium hydroxide
substances.note: Causes severe burns.

substances.name: Calcium hydroxide (slaked lime)
substances.note: Irritates skin; can damage eyes.

substances.name: Calcium oxide (quicklime)
substances.note: Gets very hot when it meets water.

substances.name: Hydrogen peroxide
substances.note: Household strength (3 %) is mild; stronger solutions burn skin and are strong oxidisers.

substances.name: Rubbing alcohol / sanitiser
substances.note: Highly flammable. Keep away from flames and hot surfaces. Not for drinking.

substances.name: Ethanol / methylated spirit
substances.note: Highly flammable liquid and vapour.

substances.name: Methanol
substances.note: Poisonous if swallowed, breathed in or absorbed through skin; can cause blindness.

substances.name: Acetone / nail polish remover
substances.note: Highly flammable. Use with ventilation.

substances.name: Hexane / petroleum solvent
substances.note: Flammable; vapour is harmful. Keep away from flames.

substances.name: Glycerol (glycerine)
substances.note: Low hazard by itself.

substances.name: Potassium permanganate
substances.note: Strong oxidiser; stains skin brown. Keep away from fuels and organic liquids.

substances.name: Potassium dichromate
substances.note: Toxic and can cause cancer. Teacher use only in most school labs.

substances.name: Ammonium nitrate
substances.note: Oxidiser. Keep away from fuels and heat.

substances.name: Iodine
substances.note: Stains; harmful if swallowed.

substances.name: Sodium metal
substances.note: Reacts violently with water. Stored under oil; teacher demonstration only.

substances.name: Potassium metal
substances.note: Reacts violently with water. Teacher demonstration only.

substances.name: Lithium metal
substances.note: Reacts with water, releasing hydrogen.

substances.name: Magnesium
substances.note: Burns with a blinding white flame; do not look straight at it.

substances.name: Cyanide salt
substances.note: Deadly poison. Not for school use.

substances.name: Washing soda
substances.note: Irritates eyes and skin.

substances.name: Copper(II) sulfate
substances.note: Harmful if swallowed; very toxic to water life.

substances.name: Silver nitrate
substances.note: Burns skin and stains it black.

substances.name: Lead(II) nitrate
substances.note: Toxic; harms the unborn child. Wash hands after use.

substances.name: Barium chloride
substances.note: Toxic if swallowed.

substances.name: Energy drink
substances.note: High in caffeine. Not recommended for children or during pregnancy.

substances.name: Alcoholic drink
substances.note: Contains alcohol.

substances.name: Paracetamol (acetaminophen)
substances.note: Never take more than the dose on the pack.

substances.name: Cold & flu remedy
substances.note: Usually contains paracetamol and a decongestant. Check the ingredients.

substances.name: Ibuprofen / anti-inflammatory
substances.note: Take with food. Not suitable for everyone; read the leaflet.

substances.name: Drowsy medicine (antihistamine, sleep aid, cough syrup)
substances.note: Can make you drowsy. Do not drive.

substances.name: Antibiotic (tetracycline / quinolone type)
substances.note: Finish the course as prescribed.

rules.title: Makes toxic gas
rules.why: Bleach and ammonia react to give chloramine gas, which burns the lungs, eyes and throat.
rules.do: Never mix or use one straight after the other. If you smell fumes, leave and get fresh air.
rules.source: CDC; Washington State Dept. of Health

rules.title: Makes chlorine gas
rules.why: Acid turns the hypochlorite in bleach into chlorine gas, which is poisonous to breathe.
rules.do: Never mix bleach with vinegar, toilet cleaner or any acid. Rinse well between products.
rules.source: CDC; Washington State Dept. of Health

rules.title: Makes toxic vapours
rules.why: Bleach reacts with alcohol to form chloroform and other harmful compounds.
rules.do: Do not mix. Use one, rinse with water, then use the other.

rules.title: Makes toxic vapours
rules.why: Bleach reacts with acetone to form chloroform, which is harmful to breathe.
rules.do: Do not mix.

rules.title: Reacts vigorously
rules.why: They react quickly and release oxygen gas and heat. In a closed container the pressure can burst it.
rules.do: Do not mix. Never store a mixture in a closed bottle.

rules.title: Makes a corrosive acid
rules.why: Hydrogen peroxide and vinegar form peracetic acid, which irritates and can burn skin, eyes and lungs.
rules.do: Do not mix in one container. Using one after the other on a surface, wiping in between, is fine.

rules.title: Explosion risk
rules.why: Hydrogen peroxide and acetone can form unstable organic peroxides that explode from heat or a knock.
rules.do: Never mix or store together.

rules.title: Violent reaction
rules.why: A strong acid and a strong alkali neutralise each other so fast that the liquid boils and spatters, and it is still corrosive.
rules.do: Never mix, and never follow one drain or toilet cleaner with another kind.

rules.title: They react and heat up
rules.why: An acid and an alkali neutralise each other and give off heat. Strong ones can spatter.
rules.do: Do not mix cleaners. In the lab, add slowly, in small amounts, wearing goggles.

rules.title: Fizzes (carbon dioxide)
rules.why: Acids react with carbonates and bicarbonates to release carbon dioxide gas: the classic fizzing volcano.
rules.do: Fine in an open container. Never seal the mixture in a closed bottle: the pressure can burst it.

rules.title: Releases hydrogen gas
rules.why: Acids react with metals such as zinc, magnesium, iron and aluminium to give hydrogen, which is flammable.
rules.do: Small amounts only, no flames nearby, good ventilation.

rules.title: Makes deadly gas
rules.why: Acid releases hydrogen cyanide gas from cyanide salts. It can kill within minutes.
rules.do: Never bring them together.

rules.title: Makes toxic gas
rules.why: Acid releases hydrogen sulfide gas (rotten-egg smell) from sulfides. It is poisonous and dulls your sense of smell.
rules.do: Fume cupboard only, under supervision.

rules.title: Violent reaction with water
rules.why: Sodium, potassium and lithium react with water to give hydrogen and heat; the hydrogen can catch fire or explode.
rules.do: Teacher demonstration only, tiny pieces, behind a safety screen.

rules.title: Explosive reaction
rules.why: Alkali metals react even more violently with acids than with water.
rules.do: Never combine.

rules.title: Gets very hot
rules.why: Diluting concentrated sulfuric acid releases a lot of heat. Adding water to the acid can make it boil and spit.
rules.do: Always add acid to water, slowly, stirring. Never water to acid.

rules.title: Gets very hot
rules.why: Quicklime reacts with water and releases enough heat to boil it.
rules.do: Add small amounts, wear goggles, keep your face away.

rules.title: Fire or explosion risk
rules.why: Nitric acid is a strong oxidiser. With alcohols, acetone and other organic liquids it can react violently, sometimes after a delay.
rules.do: Never mix or share a waste bottle.

rules.title: Fire risk
rules.why: A strong oxidiser supplies oxygen to anything that burns. Mixed with a flammable liquid it can ignite without a spark.
rules.do: Store oxidisers and flammables in separate places. Do not mix.

rules.title: Catches fire by itself
rules.why: Strong oxidisers such as potassium permanganate react with glycerol and burst into flame after a short delay.
rules.do: Do not combine outside a supervised demonstration.

rules.title: Explosive product
rules.why: Ammonia and iodine form nitrogen triiodide, which explodes at the lightest touch once dry.
rules.do: Never mix.

rules.title: Keep apart
rules.why: Cleaning products and lab chemicals can contaminate food, and are sometimes swallowed by mistake when stored beside it.
rules.do: Store chemicals away from food and drink, in their original containers.

rules.title: Keep apart
rules.why: Chemicals stored beside drinks are sometimes swallowed by mistake, especially from similar-looking bottles.
rules.do: Store chemicals away from food and drink, in their original containers.

rules.title: Keep apart
rules.why: Medicines and chemicals should not share a shelf: mix-ups and contamination happen.
rules.do: Store medicines separately, out of children's reach.

rules.title: Caffeine hides how drunk you are
rules.why: Caffeine makes you feel more alert but does not lower the alcohol in your blood, so people drink more and take more risks.
rules.do: Avoid mixing alcohol with energy drinks or other caffeine.

rules.title: Extra strain on the liver
rules.why: Heavy or regular drinking while taking paracetamol raises the risk of liver damage.
rules.do: Never exceed the stated dose. If you drink regularly, ask a pharmacist first.

rules.title: Stomach bleeding risk
rules.why: Alcohol and anti-inflammatory painkillers both irritate the stomach lining; together the risk of bleeding goes up.
rules.do: Avoid drinking while taking them, or keep to a small amount with food.

rules.title: Dangerous drowsiness
rules.why: Alcohol strengthens medicines that cause drowsiness. Together they can slow breathing and reactions badly.
rules.do: Do not drink alcohol with these medicines. Do not drive.

rules.title: Can make you very sick
rules.why: Alcohol with metronidazole can cause nausea, vomiting, flushing and a racing heart.
rules.do: Avoid alcohol during the course and for 48 hours after.

rules.title: Changes the blood-thinning effect
rules.why: Heavy drinking changes how warfarin works and raises the risk of bleeding.
rules.do: Keep to low, steady amounts and follow your clinic's advice.

rules.title: Grapefruit boosts this medicine
rules.why: Grapefruit blocks an enzyme that breaks these medicines down, so more reaches the blood and side effects increase.
rules.do: Avoid grapefruit and its juice with this medicine unless a pharmacist says it is fine.

rules.title: The iron is absorbed less
rules.why: Calcium (milk, yogurt, antacids, calcium tablets) reduces how much iron the body takes up.
rules.do: Not dangerous. Take them about 2 hours apart.
rules.source: NHS; US NIH Office of Dietary Supplements

rules.title: The iron is absorbed less
rules.why: Tannins in tea and coffee bind iron and reduce how much the body takes up.
rules.do: Not dangerous. Leave an hour or two between them.

rules.title: The antibiotic may not work as well
rules.why: Calcium in dairy foods and antacids binds these antibiotics in the gut, so less is absorbed.
rules.do: Take the antibiotic 2 hours before or several hours after dairy or antacids, as the leaflet says.

rules.title: The antibiotic may not work as well
rules.why: Iron binds these antibiotics in the gut, so less is absorbed.
rules.do: Leave several hours between them, as the leaflet says.

rules.title: A lot of caffeine
rules.why: Together these can pass the daily amount considered safe (about 400 mg for healthy adults, much less for teenagers), causing a racing heart, anxiety and poor sleep.
rules.do: Add up the caffeine on the labels. Children and teenagers should avoid energy drinks.

rules.title: Two stimulants
rules.why: Decongestants and large amounts of caffeine both raise heart rate and blood pressure.
rules.do: Avoid energy drinks while taking a decongestant.

rules.title: Both contain paracetamol
rules.why: Taking two paracetamol products together is a common cause of accidental overdose, which damages the liver.
rules.do: Take only one paracetamol product at a time and never exceed the daily maximum.

rules.title: Two anti-inflammatory painkillers
rules.why: Taking more than one anti-inflammatory raises the risk of stomach bleeding and kidney problems without relieving more pain.
rules.do: Use only one at a time.

rules.title: Serious bleeding risk
rules.why: Anti-inflammatory painkillers and aspirin increase bleeding in people taking warfarin.
rules.do: Do not take them together unless your doctor has told you to.

rules.title: If it is raw, store it apart
rules.why: Raw meat, poultry, fish and eggs can carry bacteria that spread to food eaten without cooking.
rules.do: Keep raw items sealed, on the lowest fridge shelf, away from ready-to-eat food. Use separate boards and knives.

rules.title: Safe: it only curdles
rules.why: Acid in citrus juice curdles milk, which looks odd but is harmless. Your stomach acid does the same thing.
rules.do: Fine to have together.

rules.title: Safe to eat, messy to mix
rules.why: Dropping mint sweets into a fizzy drink releases the gas all at once (the famous fountain). It is a physical effect, not a poison.
rules.do: Fine to eat and drink together. Do the fountain outdoors, never in a sealed bottle.
